politicalSituation: In October 2024, Shigeru Ishiba became Prime Minister following a closely fought LDP leadership race, leading a restructured Diet focused on rural revitalisation, wage growth outpacing inflation, structural defense modernization (raising defense spending toward 2% of GDP), energy security (restarting advanced nuclear reactors and expanding offshore wind), and mitigating the profound demographic challenge of a shrinking and super-aging population.
foreignRelations: Close security alliance with the United States; key member of the G7, Quad (with US, India, Australia), and OECD; major contributor to overseas development assistance; active advocate for a "Free and Open Indo-Pacific"; managing regional ties with China and South Korea.
military: Japan Self-Defense Forces (JSDF: Ground Self-Defense Force, Maritime Self-Defense Force with Izumo-class helicopter destroyers converted for F-35B stealth fighters, Air Self-Defense Force; highly advanced technological capabilities strictly oriented for defense).
adminDivisions: 47 prefectures (todofuken: 1 metropolis Tokyo, 1 circuit Hokkaido, 2 urban prefectures Osaka and Kyoto, and 43 rural prefectures)
history: Settled during the paleolithic Jomon period (famed for rope-patterned pottery), Japan transitioned to wet-rice agriculture and bronze-iron metalworking during the Yayoi period (c. 300 BC–300 AD). The Yamato clan consolidated imperial rule during the Kofun period. Buddhism was introduced in the 6th century, flourishing alongside indigenous Shinto traditions during the Asuka and Nara periods (when the first permanent capital was established in Nara in 710 AD). The Heian period (794–1185) in Kyoto saw a blossoming of classical aristocratic culture, yielding Murasaki Shikibu's "The Tale of Genji" (world's first novel). The rise of the warrior samurai class led to the Kamakura Shogunate in 1185 under Minamoto no Yoritomo, surviving Mongol invasions with the aid of the "Kamikaze" typhoons. After the chaotic Sengoku (Warring States) period, the "Three Great Unifiers" (Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and Tokugawa Ieyasu) reunified Japan. Tokugawa Ieyasu established the Edo Shogunate in 1603, instituting over 250 years of peaceful isolation (Sakoku) and blooming urban culture (Kabuki, Ukiyo-e woodblock prints, Haiku). In 1853, American Commodore Matthew Perry's Black Ships forced Japan to open its ports. The 1868 Meiji Restoration dismantled feudalism, restored imperial authority under Emperor Meiji, and rapidly modernized Japan into an industrial and military powerhouse. Following military expansion in Asia and catastrophic defeat in World War II (including the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945), Japan adopted a pacifist constitution and staged the miraculous post-war "Economic Miracle", rising to become the world's second-largest economy by 1968 and a global titan of technology and cultural soft power.
recentEvents2020_2026: Japan hosted the delayed Tokyo 2020 Summer Olympics in 2021, mourned the tragic assassination of former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe in July 2022, and hosted the G7 Hiroshima Summit in May 2023. In early 2024, the Bank of Japan ended its historic 17-year negative interest rate regime, and Tokyo's Nikkei 225 stock index surpassed its 1989 bubble-era all-time high. Shigeru Ishiba was elected Prime Minister in October 2024. Japan advanced semiconductor revitalization through the Rapidus 2nm chip foundry in Hokkaido and TSMC's mega-fab in Kumamoto, while preparations culminated for Expo 2025 in Osaka, Kansai.

politicalSituation: Under King Abdullah II, Jordan maintains vital political stability at the crossroads of the Middle East while implementing economic modernization and public sector reform visions. In September 2024, Jordan conducted parliamentary elections under a revised electoral law introducing dedicated political party lists. Jordan continues its historic role as the internationally recognized Hashemite Custodian of Muslim and Christian Holy Sites in Jerusalem, manages a large Syrian refugee population, and navigates regional escalations while championing Gaza humanitarian aid air-drops.
foreignRelations: Major non-NATO ally of the United States; bilateral peace treaty with Israel (1994 Wadi Araba Treaty); close diplomatic and security ties with GCC nations, Egypt, and European powers; Custodian of Jerusalem holy sites recognized under the Washington Declaration.
military: Jordanian Armed Forces (JAF / Arab Army: Royal Jordanian Army, Royal Jordanian Air Force, Royal Naval Force, and King Abdullah II Special Forces Command; highly trained professional military).
adminDivisions: 12 governorates (muhafazat) grouped into three regions: Northern, Central, and Southern
history: Inhabited since the dawn of agriculture (Neolithic settlement of 'Ain Ghazal, c. 7250 BC, famed for the world's oldest large-scale human statues). Biblical kingdoms of Ammon, Moab, and Edom flourished in the 1st millennium BC. The Nabataean Arabs established their magnificent trading capital in Petra (carved into rose-red sandstone cliffs) by the 4th century BC, controlling frankincense and spice caravan routes. Annexed by the Roman Empire under Trajan in 106 AD as Arabia Petraea, the region flourished with Greco-Roman Decapolis cities like Gerasa (Jerash) and Philadelphia (Amman). In 636 AD, the Muslim conquest triumphed at the historic Battle of the Yarmouk. The Umayyad Caliphate constructed ornate "Desert Castles" (Qusayr 'Amra). Following Crusader fortifications (Karak, Shobak), Mamluk, and Ottoman rule (1516–1918), the Great Arab Revolt erupted in 1916 led by Sharif Hussein bin Ali of Mecca. In 1921, his son Abdullah I established the Emirate of Transjordan under British mandate. Jordan achieved full sovereignty as an independent kingdom on May 25, 1946. King Hussein reigned from 1952 to 1999, guiding Jordan through the 1967 war, Black September in 1970, and signing the 1994 peace treaty with Israel. His son, King Abdullah II, ascended the throne in 1999.
recentEvents2020_2026: Jordan celebrated its centenary of statehood in 2021. Crown Prince Hussein married Princess Rajwa Al Saif in June 2023 in a grand royal wedding attended by global royalty. During 2023–2026, Jordan played a central humanitarian leadership role during the Gaza conflict, pioneering hundreds of direct aerial cargo airdrops of medical and food supplies, establishing field hospitals, and hosting international emergency relief conferences in the Dead Sea. In September 2024, Jordan held peaceful parliamentary elections under its new political reform law and appointed veteran technocrat Dr. Jafar Hassan as Prime Minister.

politicalSituation: Following the political crises of January 2022 ("Qantar"), President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev enacted comprehensive constitutional reforms establishing a single seven-year non-renewable presidential term, curtailing dynastic power, and decentralizing authority to parliament. Kazakhstan pursues a multi-vector foreign policy ("Just Kazakhstan"), balancing relations with China, Russia, the West, and fellow Turkic states, and positioning itself as the critical energy and logistics bridge of the Middle Corridor.
foreignRelations: Leading state in Central Asia; founding member of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), SCO, and EAEU; non-proliferation champion; key player in China's Belt and Road Initiative; expanding strategic partnerships with the EU and the US.
military: Armed Forces of the Republic of Kazakhstan (Ground Forces, Air Defense Forces, Naval Forces on the Caspian Sea; professionalizing military doctrine with modern unmanned systems).
adminDivisions: 17 regions (oblystar) and 3 cities of republican significance (Astana, Almaty, Shymkent), plus the Baikonur Cosmodrome leased to Russia
history: The vast Kazakh steppe was the cradle of nomadic horse-riding civilization, where horses were first domesticated by the Botai culture (c. 3500 BC). Ancient Scythians (Saka) constructed burial kurgans yielding treasures such as the "Golden Man" of Issyk. In the 13th century, Genghis Khan integrated the steppe into the Mongol Empire and the Golden Horde. In 1465, Janibek Khan and Kerei Khan broke away to establish the Kazakh Khanate, consolidating Kazakh ethnic identity and law (Zheti Zhargy under Tauke Khan) across three nomadic federations (Senior, Middle, and Junior Zhuz). Under pressure from the Dzungar invasions, the Kazakh khans gradually formed alliances with the Russian Empire during the 18th century, which culminated in full imperial annexation by the mid-19th century despite fierce rebellions led by Kenesary Khan. Following the 1917 revolution, the brief Alash Autonomy (1917–1920) was crushed by the Bolsheviks, leading to the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic. Kazakhstan suffered catastrophic collectivization famines (Asharshylyk, 1931–1933) losing over a third of its population, and later hosted the Soviet space program at Baikonur Cosmodrome (launch site of Sputnik and Yuri Gagarin). Under Nursultan Nazarbayev, Kazakhstan declared independence on December 16, 1991, voluntarily renouncing the world's fourth-largest nuclear arsenal inherited from the USSR, and moving the national capital to Astana in 1997.
recentEvents2020_2026: Following the January 2022 unrest, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev instituted the "New Kazakhstan" constitutional reforms, dismantling the Nazarbayev family's monopoly on power. Between 2023 and 2026, Kazakhstan consolidated its role as the linchpin of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (Middle Corridor), held a national referendum in October 2024 approving the construction of its first nuclear power plant, unified the country into a single time zone (UTC+5), and hosted the 5th World Nomad Games in Astana in September 2024 with over 2,500 athletes from 89 countries.

politicalSituation: In December 2023, Sheikh Meshal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah became the 17th Emir of Kuwait. In May 2024, to overcome decades of political gridlock between the elected parliament and appointed cabinet that stalled economic development, the Emir dissolved the National Assembly and suspended select constitutional articles for up to four years. The administration is focused on executing "New Kuwait / Vision 2035", reforming civil service, building Mubarak Al-Kabeer Port on Bubiyan Island, diversifying state revenues, and integrating regional rail links.
foreignRelations: Key member of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and Arab League; major non-NATO ally of the United States; historically respected regional mediator and humanitarian leader; deep security ties with the US, UK, and France; balanced commercial relations with China.
military: Kuwait Armed Forces (Kuwait Army, Kuwait Air Force with Eurofighter Typhoon and F/A-18 Super Hornet jets, Kuwait Navy, and Kuwait National Guard; hosts major US military facilities at Camp Arifjan and Ali Al Salem Air Base).
adminDivisions: 6 governorates (muhafazat): Asimah (Capital), Hawalli, Farwaniya, Ahmadi, Jahra, and Mubarak Al-Kabeer
history: In antiquity, Failaka Island was settled by the Bronze Age Dilmun civilization and later colonized by Alexander the Great's Greeks, who named it Ikaros. Modern Kuwait City was founded in the early 18th century by families of the Bani Utbah clan, including the Al Sabah family, who were chosen to lead the community in 1756. Kuwait blossomed into an independent maritime trading emporium, celebrated for pearling, boatbuilding (dhows), and long-distance maritime merchant voyages to India and East Africa. In 1899, facing Ottoman expansionism, Sheikh Mubarak Al-Sabah ("Mubarak the Great") signed an Anglo-Kuwaiti Agreement making Kuwait a British protectorate while retaining internal autonomy. In 1938, massive commercial crude oil was discovered at the Burgan Field, which proved to be the world's second-largest oil field. Kuwait achieved full independence on June 19, 1961, and established the GCC's first elected parliament and written constitution in 1962. On August 2, 1990, Iraqi forces under Saddam Hussein invaded and occupied Kuwait. A 34-nation US-led coalition liberated Kuwait in February 1991 during Operation Desert Storm. As Iraqi troops retreated, they set fire to over 700 oil wells, creating an unprecedented ecological catastrophe that was extinguished within nine months through historic international engineering heroism.
recentEvents2020_2026: Emir Sheikh Nawaf Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah passed away in December 2023, succeeded by his brother, 83-year-old Crown Prince Sheikh Meshal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah. In May 2024, Emir Meshal made the historic decision to dissolve the National Assembly and suspend select articles of the constitution to restructure governance, eliminate political paralysis, and accelerate mega-projects under "Vision 2035". In late 2024, Kuwait completed the massive $3 billion Al-Zour Refinery (one of the largest single-site petroleum refineries in the world, processing 615,000 barrels per day), completed the Sheikh Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah Causeway across Kuwait Bay, and advanced development of the Durra offshore gas field.
historicalFigures: Sheikh Abdullah Al-Salem Al-Sabah (Father of Modern Independence & Constitution)

latestElections: Parliamentary elections in November 2021; presidential election in January 2021; next presidential election scheduled for 2026
politicalSituation: Under President Sadyr Japarov, Kyrgyzstan transitioned to a centralized presidential system following the 2020 political revolution. The administration nationalized the massive Kumtor Gold Mine, brought macroeconomic stability, peacefully demarcated the historically contentious southern borders with Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, broke ground on the landmark China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) strategic railway, and advanced construction of the mega Kambar-Ata-1 hydroelectric dam.
foreignRelations: Member of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), EAEU, CSTO, SCO, and UN; close economic ties with China (lead investor in rail and road corridors) and Russia (security and labor migrant ties); deepening cooperation with Central Asian neighbors.
military: Armed Forces of the Kyrgyz Republic (Land Forces, Air Defense Forces; modernizing border defense units with Bayraktar TB2 and Akinci unmanned combat aerial vehicles).
adminDivisions: 7 regions (oblasts): Batken, Chuy, Jalal-Abad, Naryn, Osh, Talas, Issyk-Kul, and 2 independent cities (Bishkek and Osh)
history: Nomadic Yenisei Kyrgyz tribes migrated from southern Siberia to the Tian Shan mountains in the early medieval period. They established the powerful Kyrgyz Khaganate in 840 AD after defeating the Uyghur Khaganate. The territory was integrated into the Mongol Empire under Genghis Khan, later falling under the Chagatai Khanate, Dzungar Mongol dominance, and the Khanate of Kokand in the 18th century. In 1876, the Russian Empire conquered Kokand and annexed northern and southern Kyrgyzstan. Resistance culminated in the 1916 Urkun uprising. Following the Soviet Revolution, the Kara-Kyrgyz Autonomous Oblast was formed in 1924, elevated to the Kirghiz Soviet Socialist Republic in 1936. Nomadic pastoralists were forced into Soviet collective farms (kolkhozes). Kyrgyzstan declared independence on August 31, 1991. The post-Soviet era saw tumultuous political uprisings that ousted presidents in the 2005 Tulip Revolution, the 2010 revolution, and the October 2020 revolution, leading to the rise of Sadyr Japarov.
recentEvents2020_2026: In 2021, Kyrgyzstan adopted a new constitution re-establishing a strong presidential system and completed the nationalization of Kumtor Gold Mine, yielding record state budget revenues. Between 2022 and 2026, Kyrgyzstan achieved landmark historic border demarcation agreements with Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, ending decades of violent border skirmishes. In June 2024, the leaders of China, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan signed the definitive intergovernmental agreement in Beijing to construct the $4.7 billion China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) railway, and launched joint consortium construction of the 1,860 MW Kambar-Ata-1 hydropower dam with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.

constitution: Enacted in 1991; amended in 2003 and 2015
mainPoliticalParties: Lao People's Revolutionary Party (LPRP - sole legal ruling party)
latestElections: 11th National Congress of the LPRP in 2021; National Assembly election in February 2021; next elections scheduled for 2026
politicalSituation: Under President Thongloun Sisoulith and Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone, Laos successfully chaired ASEAN in 2024. The government is focused on managing public debt, stabilizing the Lao Kip through currency and fiscal tightening, maximizing economic benefits from the transformational China-Laos Railway, developing green mining and agro-forestry exports, and fulfilling its ambition to transform from a "land-locked" to a "land-linked" regional connectivity hub.
foreignRelations: Chair of ASEAN in 2024; special fraternal socialist relationship with Vietnam; comprehensive strategic partnership with China (lead investor in infrastructure, energy, and debt restructuring); strong commercial and electricity integration with Thailand.
military: Lao People's Armed Forces (LPAF: Ground Forces, Air Force, and River Patrol; political guidance provided by the LPRP).
adminDivisions: 17 provinces (khoueng) and 1 prefecture / capital municipality (Vientiane Capital)
history: In 1353, King Fa Ngum founded the Kingdom of Lan Xang Hom Khao ("The Kingdom of a Million Elephants Under the White Parasol"), establishing Theravada Buddhism as the state religion and uniting the Lao principalities with Luang Prabang as capital. Lan Xang became one of the largest empires in Southeast Asia, reaching a golden age in the 17th century under King Sourigna Vongsa. Following his death, dynastic succession disputes fragmented Lan Xang into three rival kingdoms: Luang Prabang, Vientiane, and Champasak. During the 18th and 19th centuries, these kingdoms fell under Siamese (Thai) suzerainty. In 1893, France incorporated Laos into French Indochina, preserving the royal house of Luang Prabang. Laos declared independence in 1945 following Japanese occupation, but French rule returned until full sovereignty was recognized in 1953 as the Kingdom of Laos. Caught in the Cold War and the Vietnam War, Laos became the most heavily bombed country per capita in history, as the United States dropped over two million tons of ordnance between 1964 and 1973 along the Ho Chi Minh Trail. The communist Pathet Lao movement triumphed in December 1975, abolishing the 600-year-old monarchy and establishing the Lao People's Democratic Republic under Kaysone Phomvihane. In 1986, Laos introduced the "New Economic Mechanism" (Chintanakan Mai), opening the country to market-oriented reforms and foreign investment.
recentEvents2020_2026: In December 2021, Laos inaugurated the landmark $5.9 billion, 414 km high-speed China-Laos Railway (Boten-Vientiane Railway), dramatically cutting travel times between Kunming and Vientiane, boosting regional logistics, and propelling passenger tourism to Luang Prabang and Vang Vieng. In 2024, Laos successfully assumed and executed the Chairmanship of ASEAN under the theme "ASEAN: Enhancing Connectivity and Resilience", negotiated bilateral debt relief with major creditors, expanded cross-border electricity sales to Singapore, and advanced work toward graduation from UN Least Developed Country (LDC) status by 2026.
historicalFigures: King Setthathirath (built Pha That Luang and moved capital to Vientiane in 1560)
ethnicGroups: Tai, Lue, Katang, Akha, and over 40 other distinct ethnic groups ~23.2%
religions: Theravada Buddhism ~66.0% (deeply integrated with daily civic life)
Tai folk religion / Satsana Phi (animism and spirit worship) ~30.7%
education: National University of Laos (NUOL in Vientiane), Souphanouvong University in Luang Prabang, and Champasak University in Pakse; primary education is tuition-free.
healthcare: Mittaphab Hospital and Mahosot Hospital in Vientiane; National Health Insurance (NHI) scheme subsidizes maternal and primary care for rural communities.

legislature: Parliament of Lebanon (Majlis an-Nuwwab - 128 seats equally divided 64 Christian and 64 Muslim/Druze; Speaker Nabih Berri, constitutionally a Shia Muslim)
constitution: Promulgated in 1926; revised under the 1989 Taif Agreement establishing exact confessional power-sharing parity
latestElections: Parliamentary election in May 2022; prolonged presidential vacancy and electoral deadlocks through 2024–2026
politicalSituation: Lebanon has faced a compounding polycrisis: the deep financial banking collapse of 2019, the August 2020 Beirut port explosion, a prolonged executive vacuum following the end of Michel Aoun's presidential term in 2022, and the severe military escalation between Israel and Hezbollah across southern Lebanon, the Beqaa, and southern Beirut in 2024–2026. The nation relies on its resilient global diaspora remittances (~$7 billion annually), international humanitarian support, and ongoing negotiations with the IMF for banking restructuring.
foreignRelations: Founding member of the UN and Arab League; member of the Francophonie; complex regional alignments balancing Western and Arab Gulf ties with Iranian and Syrian geopolitical influences.
military: Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF: Lebanese Army, Lebanese Air Force, Lebanese Navy; regarded as the unifying non-sectarian national institution, supported by US and French defense aid).
adminDivisions: 8 governorates (muhafazat): Beirut, Mount Lebanon, North, Akkar, Beqaa, Baalbek-Hermel, South, and Nabatieh
history: Lebanon is the historic heartland of the ancient seafaring Phoenicians (c. 2500–539 BC), who invented the world's first phonetic alphabet, built maritime trade cities in Byblos, Tyre, Sidon, and Berytus, and exported famous Tyrian purple dye and legendary cedar wood to Egyptian pharaohs and King Solomon for the Temple of Jerusalem. Conquered by Cyrus the Great, Alexander the Great, and the Romans (who built the monumental temple complex of Jupiter and Bacchus in Baalbek), the region transitioned to Christianity in late antiquity, giving rise to Saint Maron and the Maronite Church. Under Islamic rule from the 7th century, Mount Lebanon became a refuge for religious minorities, including Maronite Christians and the Druze community, who formed a unique feudal mountain coexistence. Under the Ottoman Empire (1516–1918), the Mount Lebanon Emirate flourished under Emir Fakhr al-Din II and Bashir Shihab II. Following World War I, France established the State of Greater Lebanon in 1920 under a League of Nations mandate. Lebanon achieved independence on November 22, 1943, adopting the "National Pact" (an unwritten agreement dividing executive powers among religious confessions). Known as the "Switzerland of the Middle East" and Beirut as the "Paris of the Middle East" during its 1950s–1960s banking and cultural golden age, Lebanon was devastated by the Lebanese Civil War (1975–1990). The 1989 Taif Agreement restored peace, followed by post-war reconstruction led by Prime Minister Rafic Hariri, who was assassinated in 2005, sparking the Cedar Revolution that ended the 29-year Syrian military presence.
recentEvents2020_2026: On August 4, 2020, a cataclysmic detonation of 2,750 tons of ammonium nitrate at the Port of Beirut devastated the city center, killing over 218 people, injuring 7,000, and causing billions in damage. Between 2023 and 2026, Lebanon was swept into severe cross-border warfare between Hezbollah and Israel, displacing over one million citizens from southern Lebanon, the Beqaa, and Dahieh. The international community mobilized major humanitarian conferences in Paris to assist the Lebanese Armed Forces and vulnerable civilian populations, while the private economy transitioned to full cash US-dollarization.

history: Strategically commanding the Strait of Malacca, the Malay Peninsula hosted early Hindu-Buddhist trade kingdoms such as Langkasuka and Chi Tu. In 1400, Parameswara founded the Sultanate of Malacca, which blossomed into the wealthiest trading emporium in Asia, spreading Islam and the Malay language across the archipelago. In 1511, Portuguese conqueror Afonso de Albuquerque captured Malacca, initiating centuries of European colonial presence. The Dutch East India Company ousted the Portuguese in 1641. In the late 18th century, the British East India Company established settlements in Penang (1786) and Singapore (1819), formalizing the Straits Settlements in 1826. Britain established protectorates over the Federated and Unfederated Malay States, as well as the Brooke Raj in Sarawak and the British North Borneo Company in Sabah, developing massive tin and natural rubber industries driven by Chinese and Indian immigrant labor. Following brutal Japanese occupation during World War II, the Federation of Malaya was formed, defeating a communist insurgency during the Malayan Emergency (1948–1960). Tunku Abdul Rahman ("Father of Independence") secured independence on August 31, 1957. On September 16, 1963, the Federation of Malaysia was born, incorporating Malaya, Sabah, Sarawak, and Singapore (which separated amicably in 1965). Following the 1969 ethnic riots, Malaysia instituted the New Economic Policy (NEP) to eradicate poverty and restructure society. Under Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad (1981–2003), Malaysia transformed from an agrarian exporter into a high-tech Asian tiger economy, constructing the iconic Petronas Twin Towers and Multimedia Super Corridor.
recentEvents2020_2026: In November 2022, veteran reformist Anwar Ibrahim was appointed Prime Minister, establishing a stabilizing Unity Government. In January 2024, Sultan Ibrahim of Johor was sworn in as the 17th Yang di-Pertuan Agong (King of Malaysia). Between 2023 and 2026, Malaysia emerged as a global winner in the semiconductor supply chain diversification ("China+1"), capturing over 13% of global chip assembly, testing, and packaging (ATP), attracting over $25 billion in AI hyperscale data center commitments in Johor and Cyberjaya, breaking ground on the East Coast Rail Link (ECRL), and assuming the Chairmanship of ASEAN in 2025.

Tropical depressions and wave overwash

latestElections: Presidential election in September 2023 (won by Dr. Mohamed Muizzu); parliamentary elections in April 2024 (PNC secured a supermajority)
politicalSituation: President Mohamed Muizzu assumed office in November 2023 and solidified governance with a decisive supermajority in the April 2024 parliamentary elections. His administration emphasizes national sovereignty ("Pro-Maldives" diplomatic doctrine), completing the withdrawal of unarmed Indian aviation personnel in favor of civilian operators, expanding strategic and financial ties with China and Turkey, and executing monumental land reclamation and infrastructure projects including the Ras Malé eco-smart city and the expansion of Velana International Airport to accommodate 7 million passengers.
foreignRelations: Member of the UN, Commonwealth, SAARC, and OIC; world-leading moral voice on global climate diplomacy and Small Island Developing States (SIDS); balanced diplomacy engaging China, India, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia.
military: Maldives National Defence Force (MNDF: Coast Guard, Marine Corps, Special Forces, and Air Wing; equipped with Turkish Bayraktar TB2 surveillance drones for exclusive economic zone patrols).
adminDivisions: 21 administrative divisions: 19 atolls (atholhu), 1 city (Malé), and 1 southern city (Addu City)
history: Settled as early as the 5th century BC by seafaring peoples from southern India and Sri Lanka (bringing Buddhist culture and Indo-Aryan language), the Maldives was known in antiquity as a prime source of cowrie shells (used as international currency across the Indian Ocean). In 1153 AD, the Buddhist King Dovemi converted to Islam, adopting the title Sultan Muhammad al-Adil; the archipelago remained an Islamic sultanate for over eight centuries. In 1558, the Portuguese conquered the islands, ruling brutally for fifteen years until national hero Mohamed Thakurufaanu and his brothers waged a guerrilla maritime war in their legendary boat Kalhuohfummi, expelling the Portuguese in 1573. The Maldives came under the Dutch sphere of influence in Ceylon and later became a British protected state in 1887 while maintaining domestic self-governance under its sultans. The Maldives achieved full sovereign independence from the United Kingdom on July 26, 1965, led by Prime Minister Ibrahim Nasir. Following a 1968 referendum, the sultanate was abolished and the Republic of Maldives was established. In 1972, the first tourist resort (Kurumba) opened, transforming the economy from subsistence tuna fishing into the world's premier luxury travel destination. Maumoon Abdul Gayoom served as president for thirty years (1978–2008). The 2008 democratic constitution ushered in multiparty elections, with Mohamed Nasheed elected as the first democratically elected president.
recentEvents2020_2026: The Maldives served as President of the 76th UN General Assembly (Foreign Minister Abdulla Shahid elected in 2021). In September 2023, Dr. Mohamed Muizzu won the presidency, followed by his PNC party winning a parliamentary landslide in April 2024. Between 2023 and 2026, the Maldives inaugurated new seaplane and international terminals at Velana International Airport, launched the $500 million Greater Malé Connectivity Project (GMCP / Thilamalé Bridge linking Malé, Villingili, Gulhifalhu, and Thilafushi), and commenced dredging the ambitious 1,153-hectare Ras Malé land reclamation project elevated 3 meters above sea level to secure future generations against sea-level rise.
ethnicGroups: Dhivehin (Maldivians) ~100% (homogeneous ethnic identity resulting from the mixture of South Asian, Arab, and African seafaring peoples)
Foreign resident workforce (predominantly Bangladeshi, Indian, Sri Lankan, and Filipino professionals)
religions: Sunni Islam 100% (constitutionally required for Maldivian citizenship; Shafi'i school of jurisprudence)
education: Maldives National University (MNU in Malé), Islamic University of Maldives (IUM); basic and secondary education is universal with high student-teacher ratios; expanding international tertiary scholarships.
healthcare: Indira Gandhi Memorial Hospital (IGMH in Malé), Dharumavantha Hospital (modern 25-story medical tower), and Tree Top Hospital (Hulhumalé); universal health insurance scheme (Aasandha) covers all citizens, including overseas emergency treatments in India and Sri Lanka.
socialCustoms: Communal Friday gatherings; sitting on wooden and woven coir-rope swing chairs (Joli) along sandy village lanes; fishing expeditions; afternoon tea (Sai) accompanied by savory short eats (Hedhikaa).
etiquette: Warm and polite greetings; handshakes are common, though conservative men and women may refrain from physical contact with the opposite gender; modest dress is required on local inhabited islands (bikinis and alcohol restricted to private resort islands); removing shoes when entering mosques and private homes.
nationalIdentity: Deeply anchored in the Islamic faith, the unique Dhivehi language and Thaana script, ancient seafaring mastery, boatbuilding (Dhoni), and a shared existential commitment to preserving their fragile atoll homeland.
sectors: Tourism & Hospitality 30% (direct; >60% indirect), Services & Transport 45%, Fisheries & Fish Processing 7%, Construction 18%

Pole-and-line commercial tuna fisheries and canning (MIFCO - certified sustainable by the Marine Stewardship Council)
Boat building and fiberglass Dhoni construction
Construction and coastal land reclamation

naturalResources: Pristine coral atolls and turquoise lagoons
Rich oceanic fisheries (skipjack and yellowfin tuna)

energy: Historically dependent on imported diesel generators; rapidly deploying hybrid solar-diesel systems and floating solar PV farms across atolls supported by the World Bank's ASPIRE and ARISE projects
exports: Fresh, chilled, and canned skipjack and yellowfin tuna (exporting to EU, UK, and Asian markets)
imports: Refined petroleum and aviation jet fuel
Consumer electronics and luxury resort furnishings
tradePartners: China (major infrastructure partner and free trade partner)
tourism: Surpassed 2.1 million annual international tourists (world's premier luxury "one island, one resort" model featuring overwater villas, private plunge pools, underwater restaurants, and local guesthouse tourism on islands like Maafushi).
employment: High employment in international tourism resorts, civil administration, aviation, and commercial fisheries; significant expatriate workforce in construction and service industries.
debtInflation: Maldives Monetary Authority (MMA) maintains the currency peg to the US Dollar; inflation moderate at ~2.5-3%; government implementing fiscal reforms and targeted subsidies to manage external debt service.
transport: World's largest seaplane fleet (Trans Maldivian Airways operating >65 twin-otter floatplanes); Sinamalé Bridge (China-Maldives Friendship Bridge connecting Malé to airport island Hulhulé and Hulhumalé); Thilamalé Bridge under completion; high-speed speedboats and public Raajje Transport Link (RTL) passenger ferries across atolls.
airports: Velana International Airport (MLE on Hulhulé island - modern expansion)
Gan International Airport (GAN on Addu Atoll)
ports: Port of Malé (primary commercial container port; moving to modern deepwater port on Gulhifalhu island)
internetUsage: 86.5% (nationwide 4G/5G mobile connectivity, subsea fiber-optic cables connecting all major atolls)
cuisine: Centered almost exclusively on fresh tuna (Mas) and coconut (Kurumba): Mas Huni (traditional breakfast dish of finely shredded smoked tuna mixed with grated fresh coconut, diced onions, green chilies, and lime juice, eaten with warm Roshi flatbread), Garudhiya (clear, fragrant fish broth made from fresh skipjack tuna simmered with salt, lime, and chilies, poured over steamed rice), Rihaakuru (thick, savory brown fish paste concentrated by boiling tuna broth for days), Kulhimas (spicy chili-curry fish), Hedhikaa (savory afternoon short eats: Bajiya, Gulha fried tuna dough balls, and Keemia fish rolls), and sweet Bondibai (sweetened rice or breadfruit pudding).
festivals: National Day (1 Rabi' al-Awwal)
Independence Day (July 26 - colorful school parades and cultural performances in Malé)
Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha (celebrated with Bodu Beru drumming, Koadi traditional fishing games, and community feasts)
Republic Day (November 11)
music: Bodu Beru ("Big Drum" - traditional rhythmic drumming ensemble played on wooden coconut-trunk drums, building to an ecstatic, fast-paced hypnotic crescendo accompanied by chanting and dancing, UNESCO recognized); Thaara (music brought by early Arab traders).
dance: Bodu Beru dance (vigorous, swaying rhythmic dance performed by men to drum beats); Dhandi Jehun (folk dance using colored sticks); Bolimalaafath Neshun (graceful women's dance bearing gifts).
art: Coral stone carving (exquisite relief carvings on medieval Friday Mosques built of interlocked porous coral boulders without mortar); lacquered wooden ornaments (Liyelaa Jehun) from Thulhaadhoo island; calligraphy in Thaana script.
architecture: Historic coral stone mosque architecture: Malé Old Friday Mosque (Hukuru Miskiy, built in 1656 of intricately carved coral stone with a coral minaret and lacquered wooden panels); modern architectural marvels like the Sinamalé sea bridge; eco-luxury overwater villas engineered on pilotis above lagoons.
literature: Oral folklore traditions (Dhivehi Raajjeyge Vaahaka: tales of Koimala, Bodu Thakurufaanu, and sea monsters like Rannamaari); modern poetry by Bodufenvalhuge Sidi and Ibrahim Shihab.
cinema: Local Dhivehi cinema industry producing romantic dramas and supernatural mystery films; growing international documentary focus on marine ecology and climate resilience.
sports: Football is an overwhelming national passion (Maldives National Stadium packed for the SAFF Championship; historic victory in 2008 & 2018; Ali Ashfaq "Dhagandey" legendary striker); Surfing (world-class reef breaks: Pasta Point, Sultans, Jailbreaks); Scuba diving; Volleyball; Cricket.
media: Public Service Media (PSM), Mihaaru, Sun Online, Raajje TV, and The Edition (English digital daily).
clothing: Libaas (traditional elegant red or black dress with intricate silver and gold thread embroidery called Kasabu around the neckline, worn with a black underskirt / Feyli); men wear the Sarong / Feyli with a white shirt for ceremonies; modern casual Western resort attire.
crafts: Liyelaa Jehun (traditional lacquerware on wooden vases and containers from Baa Thulhaadhoo), Kasabu Viyun (gold-thread neck embroidery), Thundu Kunaa (intricate handwoven rush mats from Gadhdhoo), and traditional Dhoni boatbuilding.

coatOfArmsDescription: A national crest depicting a graceful coconut palm tree centered behind a crescent moon and five-pointed star, flanked by two draped national flags, surmounted by a scroll inscribed with the state name "Al-Dawlat Al-Mahaldheebiyya".

Leading sectors: Tourism & Hospitality 30% (direct; >60% indirect), Services & Transport 45%, Fisheries & Fish Processing 7%, Construction 18%. Main industries: Luxury island resort tourism and hospitality, Pole-and-line commercial tuna fisheries and canning (MIFCO - certified sustainable by the Marine Stewardship Council), Boat building and fiberglass Dhoni construction, Construction and coastal land reclamation, Telecommunications and digital financial services. Key exports: Fresh, chilled, and canned skipjack and yellowfin tuna (exporting to EU, UK, and Asian markets), Fish meal and dried fish, Tourism and aviation services.
culture: Rich cultural traditions featuring cuisine (Centered almost exclusively on fresh tuna (Mas) and coconut (Kurumba): Mas Huni (traditional breakfast dish of finely shredded smoked tuna mixed with grated fresh coconut, diced onions, green chilies, and lime juice, eaten with warm Roshi flatbread), Garudhiya (clear, fragrant fish broth made from fresh skipjack tuna simmered with salt, lime, and chilies, poured over steamed rice), Rihaakuru (thick, savory brown fish paste concentrated by boiling tuna broth for days), Kulhimas (spicy chili-curry fish), Hedhikaa (savory afternoon short eats: Bajiya, Gulha fried tuna dough balls, and Keemia fish rolls), and sweet Bondibai (sweetened rice or breadfruit pudding).), traditional music and dance (Bodu Beru ("Big Drum" - traditional rhythmic drumming ensemble played on wooden coconut-trunk drums, building to an ecstatic, fast-paced hypnotic crescendo accompanied by chanting and dancing, UNESCO recognized); Thaara (music brought by early Arab traders).; Bodu Beru dance (vigorous, swaying rhythmic dance performed by men to drum beats); Dhandi Jehun (folk dance using colored sticks); Bolimalaafath Neshun (graceful women's dance bearing gifts).), literature (Oral folklore traditions (Dhivehi Raajjeyge Vaahaka: tales of Koimala, Bodu Thakurufaanu, and sea monsters like Rannamaari); modern poetry by Bodufenvalhuge Sidi and Ibrahim Shihab.), and sports (Football is an overwhelming national passion (Maldives National Stadium packed for the SAFF Championship; historic victory in 2008 & 2018; Ali Ashfaq "Dhagandey" legendary striker); Surfing (world-class reef breaks: Pasta Point, Sultans, Jailbreaks); Scuba diving; Volleyball; Cricket.).

Severe dust storms in the Gobi Desert

Pastureland degradation and desertification from overgrazing by cashmere goat herds
Deforestation in northern taiga fringes
biodiversity: Vast unbroken steppe, taiga, and Gobi desert: sanctuary for the Przewalski's horse (Takhi - the only true wild horse, successfully reintroduced to Khustain Nuruu), snow leopard, Gobi bear (Mazaalai - fewer than 50 in existence), wild Bactrian camel, saiga antelope, argali wild sheep, and Altai golden eagle
timeZone: Two time zones: Western Mongolia (UTC+07:00 in Khovd, Uvs, Bayan-Ölgii) and Central/Eastern Mongolia (UTC+08:00 in Ulaanbaatar)
languages: Mongolian (official - Khalkha dialect written in Cyrillic; traditional vertical Mongolian script undergoing official revival)
legislature: State Great Khural (Ulsyn Ikh Khural - expanded to a 126-seat parliament under constitutional amendments)
constitution: Adopted in 1992; established direct democracy, human rights, and market economy; amended in 2019 and 2023
latestElections: Parliamentary election in June 2024 under new mixed electoral system for 126 seats (MPP formed coalition government); presidential election in 2021 (next in 2027 for single 6-year term)
politicalSituation: Following the 2023 constitutional reforms that expanded parliament to 126 members under a mixed proportional-majoritarian system, Prime Minister Luvsannamsrain Oyun-Erdene led the Mongolian People's Party to victory in the June 2024 elections, forming a broad-based coalition. The government is implementing the "New Recovery Policy" and "Vision 2050", focusing on mega-mining expansion at Oyu Tolgoi (underground copper commercial production), new railway border ports to China, anti-corruption reforms in coal exports, and the national "Billion Trees" afforestation campaign.
foreignRelations: Active "Third Neighbor" foreign policy, building deep strategic, democratic, and economic partnerships with the United States, Japan, South Korea, Germany, and the European Union, while maintaining balanced, cooperative relations with immediate neighbors Russia and China; declared permanent nuclear-weapon-free status.
military: Mongolian Armed Forces (Ground Forces, Air Force, and Cyber Security; major contributor to UN Peacekeeping missions in South Sudan and worldwide; hosts annual multinational exercise Khaan Quest).
adminDivisions: 21 provinces (aimags) and 1 federal capital municipality (Ulaanbaatar), subdivided into 330 districts (sums)
history: Nomadic horse confederations dominated the Eurasian steppe for millennia, beginning with the Xiongnu Empire (c. 3rd century BC), followed by the Rouran, Turkic, and Uyghur Khaganates. In 1206, Temüjin unified the rival nomadic tribes, was proclaimed Genghis Khan ("Universal Ruler") on the banks of the Onon River, and founded the Mongol Empire. Under Genghis Khan and his successors (Ögedei, Möngke, Kublai Khan), the Mongol Empire expanded to become the largest contiguous land empire in human history, spanning from Korea and China to Central Europe, Baghdad, and the Persian Gulf. Kublai Khan founded the Yuan Dynasty in 1271 and established Beijing (Khanbaliq) as his capital. Following the collapse of the Yuan in 1368, the Mongols retreated to their homeland as the Northern Yuan Dynasty. In the 16th century, Altan Khan adopted Tibetan Gelug Buddhism, conferring the title "Dalai Lama" on Sonam Gyatso. In the late 17th century, Mongolia fell under the rule of the Manchu Qing Dynasty as Outer Mongolia. Following the collapse of the Qing Dynasty in 1911, Mongolia declared independence under the 8th Bogd Khan. In 1921, the Mongolian Revolution led by Damdin Sükhbaatar with Soviet Red Army assistance expelled Chinese and White Russian forces. In 1924, the Mongolian People's Republic was proclaimed as the world's second communist state. Under Horloogiin Choibalsan in the 1930s, the country suffered severe Stalinist purges destroying over 700 Buddhist monasteries. In 1939, Soviet and Mongolian troops defeated the Japanese Imperial Army at the Battle of Khalkhin Gol. In 1990, peaceful democratic protests in Sükhbaatar Square toppled the communist regime without bloodshed, transitioning Mongolia into a vibrant multiparty democracy.
recentEvents2020_2026: Pope Francis made a historic papal visit to Mongolia in September 2023, meeting President Khürelsükh and the small Catholic community in Ulaanbaatar. In March 2023, Rio Tinto and the Government of Mongolia inaugurated commercial underground mining operations at the massive Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold deposit. In 2024, Mongolia held landmark parliamentary elections under an expanded 126-seat assembly, inaugurated new heavy-haul coal export railways connecting Tavan Tolgoi directly to the Chinese border at Gashuunsukhait, and launched the "Go Mongolia" global tourism campaign.

Zanabazar (First Bogd Gegeen, master sculptor and Renaissance polymath)

education: National University of Mongolia (NUM), Mongolian University of Science and Technology (MUST), and Mongolian State University of Agriculture; universal basic education; literacy among nomadic herders supported by mobile boarding schools.
healthcare: First Central Hospital of Mongolia and National Cancer Center in Ulaanbaatar; expanding mobile medical caravans delivering healthcare across remote sums and aimags.
socialCustoms: Nomadic hospitality where the door of the Ger (yurt) is never locked and tea and food are always set out for passing travelers; greeting with a traditional silk scarf (Khadag) presented on open palms; sharing the snuff bottle (Khoorog); honoring the hearth fire.
etiquette: Never step on the threshold (Toono) of a Ger (seen as stepping on the host's neck); accept food and drink with the right hand supported at the elbow by the left hand; walk around the central Ger pillars clockwise; respect the sacred blue sky (Tenger).
nationalIdentity: Fierce pride in Genghis Khan and the historic Mongol Empire, the freedom of nomadic pastoral life, the bond with horses (the five sacred animals: horse, sheep, goat, cattle/yak, camel), and resilient democratic sovereignty between two authoritarian superpowers.
sectors: Mining & Extractive Industry 30%, Services 46%, Agriculture & Animal Husbandry 13%, Manufacturing & Construction 11%
industries: Copper and gold mining (Oyu Tolgoi - one of the world's largest high-grade copper mines, partnered with Rio Tinto)
Coking coal extraction (Tavan Tolgoi - massive coking coal deposits exported to China)

Molybdenum and uranium (Zuilvch Ovoo project with Orano)

Untapped wind and solar potential across the Gobi Desert
energy: Dominated by coal-fired thermal power plants in Ulaanbaatar; advancing massive wind and solar installations in the Gobi Desert to export clean power under the Asian Super Grid concept; negotiating feasibility studies for the "Power of Siberia 2" gas transit pipeline from Russia to China
exports: Coking and thermal coal (primarily transported by rail and truck to China)
Raw and processed dehaired cashmere wool

dance: Biyelgee (traditional Mongolian body and shoulder dance performed in the confined space of a Ger to the music of the Morin Khuur, expressing the daily chores of nomadic life).
art: Zanabazar's exquisite gilded bronze Buddhist sculptures (the "Michelangelo of Asia"); Thangka scroll painting; Appliqué silk embroidery; intricate silver bowls (Ayaga); traditional calligraphy in vertical Mongolian script (UNESCO).

name: Myanmar
officialName: Republic of the Union of Myanmar
nativeName: ပြည်ထောင်စု သမ္မတ မြန်မာနိုင်ငံတော် (Pyidaunzu Thanmăda Myăma Nainngandaw)
nationalDay: January 4 (Independence Day from Britain in 1948) / National Day (celebrated in late autumn according to lunar calendar)
nationalAnthem: Kaba Ma Kyei (Till the End of the World, Myanmar)
motto: None (Unofficial)
coastline: 1,930 km (Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea coastline, including the Mergui Archipelago)
highestPoint: Hkakabo Razi (5,881 m in northern Kachin State - highest peak in Southeast Asia)
longestRiver: Irrawaddy River (Ayeyarwady, 2,288 km total; the lifeblood of Myanmar flowing north to south into the vast Irrawaddy Delta)
majorLakes: Inle Lake (famous for leg-rowing fishermen and floating gardens)
Indawgyi Lake (largest natural lake in Southeast Asia)
Rih Dil (heart-shaped lake in Chin State)

naturalHazards: Severe tropical cyclones from the Bay of Bengal (e.g., Cyclone Nargis in 2008, Cyclone Mocha in 2023)
Earthquakes along the active Sagaing Fault line
Monsoon flooding and landslides

Illegal artisanal jade, gold, and rare earth mining causing environmental degradation
Mangrove loss in the Irrawaddy Delta
Freshwater siltation in Inle Lake
biodiversity: Vast biodiversity spanning Himalayan snows to tropical coral reefs: home to the Irrawaddy dolphin, Indochinese tiger, Asian elephant, red panda, sun bear, Hoolock gibbon, and green sea turtles
languages: Burmese (Bamar - official Sino-Tibetan language with unique rounded script)
government: Unitary military junta administration (State Administration Council - SAC) facing nationwide armed opposition and parallel National Unity Government (NUG)
headOfState: Acting President Myint Swe / SAC Chairman Senior General Min Aung Hlaing
headOfGovernment: Prime Minister Senior General Min Aung Hlaing
legislature: Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (Assembly of the Union - suspended following the February 2021 coup)
constitution: Enacted in 2008; drafted under military supervision guaranteeing 25% of parliamentary seats and key security ministries to the armed forces
mainPoliticalParties: Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP - military-aligned); National League for Democracy (NLD - dissolved by junta commission in 2023; leaders Aung San Suu Kyi and Win Myint detained); National Unity Government (NUG parallel administration); ethnic political parties
latestElections: November 2020 general election (overwhelmingly won by the NLD, subsequently annulled by the military); military regime repeatedly proposed multi-party elections postponed due to state of emergency and nationwide civil war
politicalSituation: Since the military coup of February 1, 2021 that ousted the democratically elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar has been engulfed in a multi-front civil war. A nationwide popular resistance movement, comprising the People's Defence Forces (PDF) aligned with the National Unity Government (NUG) and long-standing Ethnic Armed Organizations (EAOs), launched coordinated offensives. The historic "Operation 1027" (launched in late 2023 by the Three Brotherhood Alliance in northern Shan State and Rakhine) captured dozens of towns, border trade crossings to China, and regional military commands, severely contracting the junta's territorial control and deepening economic distress through 2024–2026.
foreignRelations: Subject to broad Western economic, arms, and financial sanctions; maintains essential diplomatic, energy, and defense relationships with China and Russia; complex relations within ASEAN (which bars junta political representatives from high-level summits under the stalled Five-Point Consensus); commercial engagement with Thailand and India.
military: Tatmadaw (Myanmar Armed Forces: Myanmar Army, Myanmar Air Force, Myanmar Navy; facing severe manpower shortages leading to the enforcement of mandatory conscription in 2024; opposed by coalition EAOs and PDF forces).
adminDivisions: 7 regions (dominated by Bamar majority: Ayeyarwady, Bago, Magway, Mandalay, Sagaing, Tanintharyi, Yangon) and 7 ethnic states (Chin, Kachin, Kayah, Kayin, Mon, Rakhine, Shan), plus the Naypyidaw Union Territory
history: Inhabited since antiquity by Pyu city-states and Mon kingdoms, Myanmar was unified in 1044 AD by King Anawrahta, founder of the Pagan (Bagan) Empire. He embraced Theravada Buddhism, and during the next two centuries, over 10,000 Buddhist temples and stupas were constructed across the Bagan plains. Mongol invasions under Kublai Khan shattered Bagan in 1287, leading to divided regional kingdoms (Ava, Hanthawaddy Pegu, Mrauk U in Rakhine). King Bayinnaung of the Taungoo Dynasty reunified the realm in the 16th century, creating the largest empire in Southeast Asian history. The Konbaung Dynasty (1752–1885) under Alaungpaya expanded Burmese dominion before clashing with the British East India Company. Through three Anglo-Burmese Wars (1824–1885), Britain colonized Burma, incorporating it as a province of British India, culminating in the exile of the last king, Thibaw, in 1885. General Aung San negotiated independence following World War II but was tragically assassinated in July 1947 alongside six cabinet colleagues. Burma achieved independence on January 4, 1948, under Prime Minister U Nu, immediately confronting armed communist and ethnic insurgencies. In 1962, General Ne Win led a military coup, establishing the isolationist "Burmese Way to Socialism". The nationwide 1988 pro-democracy uprising (8888 Uprising) gave rise to Aung San Suu Kyi and the National League for Democracy (NLD). A brief period of political opening and quasi-civilian democratic transition occurred between 2011 and 2020, bringing rapid economic modernization before the military abruptly seized power again in February 2021.
recentEvents2020_2026: The February 2021 military coup triggered nationwide strikes (Civil Disobedience Movement - CDM) and an unprecedented armed resistance movement combining young urban pro-democracy fighters with experienced ethnic armed armies. In October 2023, the Three Brotherhood Alliance launched "Operation 1027", capturing critical northern border crossings and towns in Shan State and Rakhine. Through 2024–2026, the military junta enforced nationwide conscription, faced intense fuel shortages and inflation exceeding 30%, lost control over major frontier trade routes to China and Thailand, while Aung San Suu Kyi remained detained under administrative sentences.
historicalFigures: Aung San Suu Kyi (Nobel Peace laureate)
U Thant (third Secretary-General of the United Nations)
ethnicGroups: Kachin, Chin, Kayah, and over 100 other recognized indigenous nationalities ~5%
religions: Christianity (Baptist, Catholic - widespread in Chin, Kachin, and Karen states) ~6.2%
Islam (predominantly in Yangon and Rakhine State) ~4.3%
education: Historic universities include University of Yangon ("Rangoon University", historic cradle of student independence protests) and Mandalay University; higher education severely disrupted post-2021 by student and faculty boycotts.
healthcare: Public hospital system supplemented by private clinics; facing severe personnel shortages and strain due to civil conflict; international humanitarian agencies delivering emergency care in border conflict zones.
socialCustoms: Wearing Thanaka (fragrant golden-yellow paste ground from tree bark applied to cheeks and foreheads as natural sun protection, cooling cosmetic, and skin treatment); widespread chewing of Kun-ya (betel nut quid with slaked lime and tobacco); communal novitiation ceremonies (Shinbyu) for young boys entering the Buddhist monkhood.
etiquette: Showing deep reverence to monks and elders; touching one's right elbow with the left hand when giving or receiving money; never touching another person's head or stepping over anyone's body; removing shoes and socks completely before entering temple grounds and pagodas.
nationalIdentity: A complex tapestry of deep Theravada Buddhist devotion, sacred pagoda construction, pride in ancient royal empires (Bagan, Taungoo), and an ongoing, heroic struggle for federal democracy and ethnic self-determination.

agriculture: Rice (Irrawaddy Delta is the historic "rice bowl" of Burma)
Pulses and beans (world-leading exporter of black gram and pigeon peas)

dance: Yein (graceful synchronized ensemble dance performed by troupes of women during Thingyan); traditional Marionette theatre (Yoke thé - puppetry that historically influenced classical dance movements).
art: Pan Sel Myo (the Ten Traditional Arts: lacquerware, gold leaf pounding, bronze casting, stone carving, woodcarving, painting, stucco, blacksmithing, turnery, and silversmithing); exquisite gold leaf applied to the Mahamuni and Shwedagon statues.
architecture: Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon (magnificent 99-meter golden pagoda encrusted with over 7,000 diamonds, rubies, and sapphires, crowned by a 76-carat diamond); the monumental brick temples of Bagan (Ananda Temple, Thatbyinnyu, Dhammayangyi); wooden monasteries (Shwenandaw Monastery in Mandalay); U Bein Bridge (world's oldest and longest teakwood bridge, 1.2 km).
literature: Classical Buddhist treatises and court poetry (Yadu); modern literature of Thakin Kodaw Hmaing; acclaimed contemporary writers like Pascal Khoo Thwe ("From the Land of Green Ghosts") and Ludu Daw Amar.
cinema: Historic cinema industry founded in 1920 (first feature "Love and Liquor"); contemporary independent cinema flourishing underground and among diaspora filmmakers documentarians capturing the post-coup struggle.

Air quality pollution in the bowl-shaped Kathmandu Valley
Deforestation and slope erosion in the Churia hills
biodiversity: Astonishing biodiversity spanning tropical jungles to alpine peaks: home to the Royal Bengal tiger, greater one-horned rhinoceros (Chitwan National Park), snow leopard, red panda, Asian elephant, Himalayan tahr, and over 880 bird species
timeZone: UTC+05:45 (NPT - unique 45-minute offset based on the meridian of Gauri Sankar mountain)
languages: Nepali (official - Indo-Aryan language written in Devanagari script)
currency: Nepalese Rupee (NPR, रू - pegged at 1.60 NPR to 1 Indian Rupee)
legislature: Federal Parliament of Nepal (Sanghiya Sansad: National Assembly and House of Representatives / Pratinidhi Sabha)
constitution: Promulgated on September 20, 2015; established federal secular republic with seven provinces
mainPoliticalParties: Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist–Leninist - CPN-UML)
Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre - CPN-MC)
latestElections: Federal parliamentary elections in November 2022; coalition government reshuffle in July 2024 with K.P. Sharma Oli assuming the premiership; next general elections scheduled for 2027
politicalSituation: In July 2024, CPN-UML leader K.P. Sharma Oli formed a major coalition government with the center-left Nepali Congress party, providing parliamentary stability. The administration prioritizes constitutional governance, completing the transitional justice truth and reconciliation commissions from the 1996–2006 civil conflict, expanding cross-border hydroelectric sales to India and Bangladesh, upgrading tourist and transport infrastructure, and preparing for graduation from UN Least Developed Country (LDC) status in 2026.
foreignRelations: Maintains strict non-alignment and balanced diplomacy ("a yam between two boulders") between immediate giant neighbors India and China; major troop contributor to United Nations Peacekeeping operations worldwide; member of SAARC and BIMSTEC.
military: Nepali Army (dedicated ground defense force; international peacekeeping pillar; historic lineage of the legendary Gurkha warriors).
adminDivisions: 7 provinces: Koshi, Madhesh, Bagmati, Gandaki, Lumbini, Karnali, and Sudurpashchim, subdivided into 77 districts
history: Settled since antiquity, the Kathmandu Valley flourished under the Kirat, Licchavi (4th–8th century AD, classical golden age of architecture), and Malla dynasties (12th–18th century). The Mallas divided the valley into three rival artistic city-kingdoms: Kathmandu (Kantipur), Patan (Lalitpur), and Bhaktapur, building the UNESCO Durbar Squares. Lumbini in southern Nepal is celebrated worldwide as the sacred birthplace of Siddhartha Gautama (Gautama Buddha, born c. 563 BC). In 1768, King Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha unified the disparate hill states and kingdoms, establishing the modern Kingdom of Nepal. Following the Anglo-Nepalese War (1814–1816) and the Treaty of Sugauli, the British Empire recognized Nepalese sovereignty while recruiting fearless Nepali soldiers as the famed British Gurkhas. The 1846 Kot Massacre brought the autocratic Rana Dynasty to power, ruling as hereditary prime ministers for 104 years until King Tribhuvan restored royal authority in 1951. King Mahendra introduced the non-party Panchayat system in 1960. Mass pro-democracy protests (Jana Andolan I) in 1990 restored multiparty constitutional monarchy under King Birendra. In June 2001, the tragic Royal Massacre wiped out King Birendra and his immediate family. Meanwhile, a decade-long Maoist insurgency (1996–2006) claimed over 17,000 lives, culminating in the 2006 Comprehensive Peace Accord, the abolition of the 240-year-old monarchy in 2008, and the birth of the Federal Democratic Republic of Nepal.
recentEvents2020_2026: Nepal inaugurated the Pokhara International Airport and Gautam Buddha International Airport in Bhairahawa in 2022–2023. In July 2024, K.P. Sharma Oli returned as Prime Minister leading a stable CPN-UML and Nepali Congress grand coalition. In late 2024, Nepal signed a historic trilateral power agreement with India and Bangladesh to export 40 MW of hydroelectricity across Indian transmission lines to Bangladesh. Nepal also finalized transitional justice legislation for victims of the civil conflict and made final preparations for graduation from UN Least Developed Country (LDC) status in 2026.
historicalFigures: Gautama Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama, born in Lumbini)
Tenzing Norgay Sherpa (first to summit Everest with Edmund Hillary in 1953)
Araniko (master Newar architect who built the White Pagoda in Beijing)
Bhanubhakta Acharya (Adi Kabi - Father of Nepali Literature)
ethnicGroups: Rai, Gurung, Damai, Limbu, Sherpa, and over 120 other caste and ethnic groups ~33.5%
religions: Hinduism ~81.2% (profoundly influential; Nepal was historically the world's only official Hindu kingdom until 2006)
urbanization: 22.5% (rapidly suburbanizing around Kathmandu and the Terai)
education: Tribhuvan University (oldest and largest public university in Nepal, founded 1959), Kathmandu University (KU in Dhulikhel - premier private institution), and Pokhara University; renowned international medical and engineering colleges.
healthcare: Bir Hospital, Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital (TUTH), and Patan Hospital; expanding National Health Insurance Board (NHIB) subsidizing rural health clinics and hospital coverage.
socialCustoms: Namaste greeting with pressed palms and a slight bow; deep family hospitality; celebrating Dashain (15-day triumph of good over evil) with elders applying red Tika and Jamara to foreheads; flying kites and playing on bamboo swings (Ping); respecting sacred cows.
etiquette: Never step over someone's outstretched legs; removing shoes when entering private homes and temples; using the right hand for eating and giving gifts; touching feet of parents and elders for blessings (Dhok).
nationalIdentity: Defined by Mount Everest (Sagarmatha) and the Himalayas, the birthplace of Gautama Buddha at Lumbini, the non-rectangular national flag, martial honor of the Gurkhas, syncretic harmony between Hinduism and Buddhism, and sovereign independence never colonized by a foreign power.
sectors: Services 62% (tourism, banking, remittances, and telecommunications), Agriculture 24%, Industry & Hydropower 14%
industries: Hydroelectric power generation (rapidly expanding Himalayan run-of-the-river projects: Upper Tamakoshi, Arun III)
Mountaineering, trekking, and eco-tourism
Cement and construction materials manufacturing
Textiles, carpets, and pashmina shawls
Agro-processing (tea, cardamom, ginger, noodles)

agriculture: Maize, wheat, and millet in hill terraces
Large cardamom (world's #1 producer of black cardamom / Alaichi)
Buffalo milk and dairy (Chhurpi hard cheese)

Timber and medicinal Himalayan herbs (Yarsagumba - caterpillar fungus)
energy: Virtually 100% domestic electricity produced by renewable run-of-the-river hydropower; massive exporter of clean electricity to India during monsoon months; expanding cross-border transmission lines to Bangladesh
exports: Refined palm oil and soybean oil
imports: Petroleum fuels and LPG (from India via Motihari-Amlekhgunj pipeline)

tourism: Surpassed 1.3 million international tourists drawn to mountaineering expeditions on Mount Everest and the Annapurna Circuit, trekking in Langtang and Manaslu, serene lakes and paragliding in Pokhara, wildlife jungle safaris in Chitwan (rhinos and tigers), and ancient Durbar Squares of Kathmandu.
employment: Remittances sent by over 3 million Nepali migrant workers in the Gulf states, Malaysia, and worldwide exceed $10 billion annually (~25% of GDP); growing employment in tourism, civil engineering, and IT.
debtInflation: Nepal Rastra Bank maintains the currency peg to the Indian Rupee (1.60 NPR = 1 INR); robust foreign exchange reserves exceeding $14 billion; inflation tracking Indian price levels around 5-6%.
transport: Tribhuvan Highway and Prithvi Highway connecting Kathmandu to the Terai and Pokhara; Mugling-Pokhara highway four-lane expansion; Narayangarh-Butwal highway; domestic STOL mountain flights (Lukla Tenzing-Hillary Airport, gateway to Everest).
ports: Landlocked; relies on Indian seaports of Kolkata/Haldia and Visakhapatnam for international container maritime cargo via the Birgunj Integrated Check Post (ICP) rail dry port
internetUsage: 52.5% (expanding fiber-to-the-home networks and 4G/5G mobile connectivity, widespread digital payments via eSewa, Khalti, and Fonepay QR)

festivals: Dashain / Bijaya Dashami (grandest 15-day national festival celebrating the victory of goddess Durga)
Tihar / Deepawali (Festival of Lights: five days honoring crows, dogs, cows, oxen, and sisters through Bhai Tika)
Holi (Festival of Colors)
Maha Shivaratri (massive gathering of hundreds of thousands of sadhus and pilgrims at Pashupatinath Temple)
Buddha Jayanti (celebrating Buddha's birth in Lumbini)

Teej (women's festival in red sarees)

dance: Maruni dance, Lakhey masked demon dance (performed during Indra Jatra in Kathmandu), Tamang Selo, Chandi dance (Rai community), and Sorathi dance.
art: Newar Paubha painting (intricate traditional religious scroll painting depicting Hindu and Buddhist deities); Newari woodcarving (intricately carved wooden peacocks, struts, and window lattices of Bhaktapur); lost-wax bronze metal sculpture; Thangka painting.
architecture: Distinctive multi-roofed Newar pagoda temple architecture (Nyatapola Temple in Bhaktapur, Kasthamandap); massive hemispherical Buddhist stupas with serene all-seeing eyes of the Buddha (Boudhanath and Swayambhunath); ancient Durbar Squares of Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur.
literature: Bhanubhakta Acharya (translated the Valmiki Ramayana into vernacular Nepali, unifying the literary language); Laxmi Prasad Devkota ("The Great Poet" / Mahakavi: "Muna Madan", the best-selling book in Nepali literature); Parijat ("Siris ko Phool" / The Blue Mimosa); modern authors Samrat Upadhyay and Manjushree Thapa.
cinema: Emerging Nepali cinema ("Kollywood"); acclaimed international festival-winning independent directors: Min Bahadur Bham ("The Black Hen", "Shambhala" - historic premiere at the 2024 Berlin International Film Festival) and Nabin Subba ("A Road to a Village").
sports: Cricket is an immense national passion (the Nepali national cricket team "Rhinos" qualified for the ICC Men's T20 World Cup in 2024 amidst wild domestic euphoria); Football (packed Dasharath Stadium); Mountaineering and Trail Running (world-record mountain athlete Mira Rai; Nirmal "Nimsdai" Purja who summited all 14 eight-thousanders in 6 months); Volleyball (national sport).
media: Kantipur Publications, The Kathmandu Post, Republica, Onlinekhabar, Setopati, Nepal Television (NTV), and Kantipur TV.
clothing: Daura-Suruwal (traditional tunic and trousers with tailored Dhaka topi geometric woven hat and coat for men); Gunyou-Cholo or vibrant red and green Sarees for women; Bakkhu wool coats and Pangden aprons worn by Sherpa women in the high mountains.
crafts: Handwoven Dhaka fabric (Dhaka topi hats and shawls from Palpa), handmade Lokta Daphne bush paper, hand-knotted Tibetan wool carpets, silver filigree jewelry, and singing bowls.
worldHeritageSites: Kathmandu Valley (seven monument zones: Durbar Squares of Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur; Swayambhunath, Boudhanath, Pashupatinath, Changu Narayan)
Lumbini, the Birthplace of the Lord Buddha

flagDescription: The world's only non-quadrilateral national flag: a combination of two vertical red triangular pennants bordered in deep blue; the upper pennant bears a white stylized crescent moon with eight rays, and the lower pennant bears a white twelve-pointed sun (symbolizing the desire for the nation to endure as long as the sun and moon).
coatOfArmsDescription: A circular emblem depicting Mount Everest in the background, a white map of Nepal on green hills, joined male and female hands symbolizing gender equality, framed by sheaves of rice and a garland of red rhododendrons, topped by the national flag, inscribed below with the national motto "Mother and Motherland Are Greater Than Heaven".
